extracted.intended_audience: hospital coders, Medicare payment policy analysts, MS-DRG reviewers, device manufacturers and other stakeholders requesting MS-DRG modifications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating requests to create, split, reassign, or otherwise modify MS-DRGs (including procedure code reassignment and new procedure codes) for the IPPS/LTCH PPS; describes data, analytic, and clinical-coherence criteria CMS uses. Focus is on how CMS decides whether to split a base MS-DRG, create a new MS-DRG, or reassign procedure/diagnosis codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five criteria for splitting MS-DRG (overall requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, once the decision has been made to propose to make further modifications to the MS-DRGs ... all five criteria must be met for the base MS-DRG to be split (or subdivided) by a CC subgroup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All five criteria must be satisfied before splitting a base MS-DRG into severity levels. When evaluating requests to split an existing base MS-DRG into severity levels, CMS typically analyzes the most recent two years of MedPAR claims data. If the five criteria are not all met for a three-way split, CMS next evaluates two-way splits. If the criteria for both two-way splits fail, a split would generally not be warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria 1 and 2: Volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume (Criteria 1 and 2) is used as part of the evaluation of subgroup differences when considering splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each subgroup (MCC, CC, NonCC for three-way; or the two two-way splits) is analyzed in relation to the other subgroup(s) using the volume criteria. Sufficient case counts are necessary to support stable classification decisions; low volume may preclude creating new MS-DRGs or warrant further analysis of clinical/resource patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria 3 and 4: Average cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Average cost (Criteria 3 and 4) is evaluated to determine whether subgroup resource use differs meaningfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS compares average costs across subgroups (and versus the full MS-DRG) to assess whether differences justify splitting. CMS recognizes limitations in claims data for attributing cost differences specifically to a procedure versus underlying severity or other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria 5: Reduction in variance (statistical fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction in variance (Criteria 5) is evaluated to determine whether subdivision meaningfully reduces cost variance within groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS uses measures of fit (e.g., R2) to assess whether a proposed split reduces within-group variance. If multiple valid two-way splits meet all criteria, CMS will apply the two-way split with the highest R2 value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-way split evaluation process (MCC, CC, NonCC)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a three-way split, a base MS-DRG is initially subdivided into MCC, CC, and NonCC subgroups and each subgroup is analyzed in relation to the other two using volume, average cost, and reduction in variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the three-way split fails any of the five criteria, CMS then considers two-way splits. When applying criteria for a three-way split, CMS typically analyzes the most recent two years of MedPAR data to avoid decisions based on an isolated year's fluctuation and to validate established severity levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way split evaluation process (1_23 and 12_3)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a three-way split is not supported, CMS evaluates two-way splits: either 'with MCC' vs 'without MCC' (1_23) or 'with CC/MCC' vs 'without CC/MCC' (12_3), applying the same volume, average cost, and reduction-in-variance criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both two-way splits fail to meet the criteria, a split is generally not warranted. If both two-way splits meet all five criteria, CMS selects the two-way split with the highest R2. If a request specifies one of the two-way splits, CMS will evaluate both two-way splits (1_23 and 12_3) but will not also evaluate a three-way split in response to that specific request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-year selection: one-year vs two-year analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For requests to create a new MS-DRG, CMS typically evaluates the most recent year of MedPAR claims data; for requests to split an existing base MS-DRG, CMS typically analyzes the most recent two years of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two years of data are used for splitting to compare year-to-year results and avoid determinations based on an isolated year's fluctuation and to validate established severity levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of predecessor codes and clinical/resource factors when no claims data exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When new procedure codes are effective and thus absent from the claims data, CMS reviews the predecessor code and MS-DRG assignment most closely associated with the new procedure code and, in the absence of claims data, considers other relevant factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other relevant factors include severity of illness, treatment difficulty, complexity of service, and resources utilized in diagnosis and/or treatment. This process does not automatically assign the new code to the same MS-DRG or designation (O.R. vs non-O.R.) as the predecessor code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for substantial case counts (sufficiency of claims data)
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS prefers to have a substantial number of cases in an MS-DRG because larger clinically cohesive groups provide greater stability for annual updates to relative payment weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are only a few patients in a respective MS-DRG, CMS considers potential changes in clinical characteristics, treatment patterns, or resource utilization and may further analyze reclassification options. Lack of sufficient claims volume can preclude creating a new MS-DRG or may prompt reassignment of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of clinical coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of clinical coherence requires that patient characteristics included in the definition of each MS-DRG relate to a common organ system or etiology and that a specific medical specialty should typically provide care to the patients in the DRG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS assesses whether diagnoses/procedures are clinically aligned with the MDC and MS-DRG; reassignment that would break clinical coherence (e.g., moving diagnoses into a different MDC causing unrelated OR procedure assignments) is avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding unintended consequences (unrelated O.R. procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS considers whether moving diagnosis codes between MDCs would inadvertently cause cases with certain O.R. procedures to be assigned to an 'unrelated operating room procedures' surgical class and thus to unrelated MS-DRGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS analyzes counts of cases and types of O.R. procedures that would be affected (for example, how many cases with pulmonary embolism report an O.R. procedure) to assess the impact of reassignment and to avoid unintended reclassification effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical hierarchy ordering principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The surgical hierarchy is an ordering of surgical classes from most resource-intensive to least resource-intensive used to ensure cases with multiple surgical procedures are assigned to the MS-DRG associated with the most resource-intensive surgical class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS uses the surgical hierarchy when considering reassignment within an MDC to ensure MS-DRG assignment reflects the most resource-intensive operative class present on the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: MS-DRG system as a system of averages (expect within-group variance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MS-DRG system is a system of averages and it is expected that within diagnostic related groups some cases may demonstrate higher than average costs, while other cases may demonstrate lower than average costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS recognizes outlier/extraordinary cost mechanisms (section 1886(d)(5)(A) of the Act) provide additional payments for cases incurring extraordinarily high costs and considers this when assessing whether reclassification is necessary for relatively small high-cost subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude procedure codes that are ubiquitously present from subgroup analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a procedure code (e.g., 5A0221D for assistance with an impeller pump) is always coded in the identified cases, CMS may exclude it from analysis because its presence would be expected across all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude such ubiquitous codes from comparative analysis of procedure subsets to avoid skewing results; instead analyze the distinguishing procedure codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution caution: distinguish procedure resource use from patient severity and admission circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims data may not allow CMS to ascertain the additional resource use specifically attributable to a procedure (e.g., insertion of a heart assist device) versus resource use attributable to the severity of illness or other admission circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS reviews principal diagnoses and diagnostic subcodes to evaluate the extent to which higher costs are due to underlying diagnoses (e.g., different pulmonary embolism codes) versus the procedure itself, and acknowledges wide variance across small sample subsets may limit conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of broader MDC-level impacts when reassigning diagnoses
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS analyzes how reassignment of diagnoses between MDCs would affect the assignment of many cases (e.g., number of cases with an O.R. procedure and a principal diagnosis in a given MDC) and whether such reassignment would have undesirable widespread effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS uses counts (e.g., thousands of cases vs a handful) and the distribution of O.R. procedures to judge whether moving diagnoses would produce unintended reassignments that reduce clinical coherence or misgroup large numbers of cases.
